To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of biomarkers in the evaluation of acute stroke treatments can be used to reduce sample size requirements for phase III clinical trials, and to provide supportive evidence of efficacy to obtain regulatory approval.

the FDA modernization act provides a framework for the development of acute stroke therapies that are based on a phase IIB study with a biomarker endpoint, followed by a large phase III trial that includes the same biomarker and a clinical endpoint.

the FDA modernization act provides an opportunity to develop new acute stroke treatments by coupling phase IIB imaging-based trials with phase III clinical trials, that such an approach is feasible and can be optimized using ‘pick the winner strategies’ and that the FDA has approved such an approach.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods and statistical tools for evaluating potential acute stroke therapies.
developing statistical methods to design phase IIB studies for acute stroke therapies, and to evaluate the evidence provided by such trials to support phase III trials.
developing new approaches for evaluating the safety and efficacy of drugs for treating acute stroke.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the FDA modernization act provides a framework to develop new therapies for acute ischemic cerebrovascular disease, but the act does not provide a specific pathway to obtain approval for such a drug.
an imaging-based phase 2 study could potentially provide the evidence needed to support a phase 3 study.

the FDA modernization act, coupled with a statistical design that modifies the probability of randomization to the ‘winner’ treatment strategy, provides a new pathway for evaluating potential acute stroke therapies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of biomarker endpoints in the development of new acute ischemic stroke therapies is a promising and potentially cost-effective strategy.

the use of imaging-based biomarkers in phase IIB trials may be a viable option to provide supportive evidence for new drug applications, and that the design of phase IIB trials can be optimized to minimize sample size requirements.
a phase IIB study of an imaging-based biomarker can provide supportive evidence to obtain FDA approval for a new drug.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to design phase IIB studies with a small sample size that can provide supportive evidence of efficacy and reduce the sample size required in the subsequent phase III trial.
a phase IIB study can be designed to demonstrate a treatment effect on imaging endpoints and that such a study can be used as supportive evidence for a subsequent phase III clinical outcome trial.
the use of a biomarker-based phase IIB trial can reduce the size and duration of a phase III trial and thereby accelerate the drug approval process.
